title: They Had Not Won a Title in Two Years. Then Satwik and Chirag Beat the World Champions in Singapore.
excerpt: India's top doubles pair ended a painful drought by stunning Kim Won-ho and Seo Seung-jae in the semifinals, then outclassed Indonesia's Alfian and Fikri in the final to win the Singapore Open Super 750.
body:
The last time Satwiksairaj Rankireddy and Chirag Shetty lifted a trophy together, the Paris Olympics were still months away. That was the French Open in March 2024. What followed was a stretch of frustration that neither of them — former world No. 1, Asian Games gold medallists, Thomas Cup winners — had experienced before in their partnership.

Injuries. Personal setbacks. A Thomas Cup campaign where Satwik's shoulder was held together more by willpower than by physiology. A Thailand Open final that slipped away. Two years without silverware is an eternity in the career of any elite athlete, but for a pair that had grown accustomed to winning at the highest level, it stung differently.

"I always believed that eventually the win will come," Chirag said after their Singapore Open triumph on May 31. "But it was just a matter of time. We needed to keep pushing ourselves. We've done it before, and we know how to win titles."

## The Semifinal That Changed Everything

The defining moment of their Singapore Open campaign came not in the final but one round earlier. Standing across the net were Kim Won-ho and Seo Seung-jae — South Korea's reigning world champions, riding a 34-match winning streak, and holders of a 2-0 head-to-head record against the Indian duo.

Satwik and Chirag trailed 8-13 in the first game. They fell behind again at 13-17. On most days over the past two years, those moments would have spelled the end of a run. Not this time.

"Nobody on the circuit is unbeatable," Chirag said. "When we entered the court, we knew that if we keep things simple and play to the plan, we stand a chance."

They won the first game 21-19 after mounting a breathtaking comeback. The second game was more controlled: 21-18. In 52 minutes, the Indians had ended one of the longest winning streaks in men's doubles badminton and announced that the best version of themselves was back.

## The Final: Clinical and Complete

In the final against Indonesia's Fajar Alfian and Muhammad Shohibul Fikri, the Indians lost the first game 18-21 but showed the kind of composure that defines championship pairs. They levelled with a dominant 21-17 second game and then ran away with the decider 21-16. The Singapore Open Super 750 trophy — worth 11,000 ranking points and $74,000 in prize money — was theirs.

For NRI fans watching from the US, UK, and beyond, it was a reminder that Indian badminton's depth extends well beyond PV Sindhu. Satwik and Chirag have quietly built one of the most decorated partnerships in the sport's history: a Thomas Cup title, Asian Games gold, Commonwealth Games gold, multiple Super 750 and Super 500 trophies, and a career-high world ranking of No. 1.

## What Comes Next: World Championships and Asian Games

The victory has set the stage for an ambitious second half of 2026. Chirag revealed they pulled out of the Indonesia Open immediately after Singapore to allow Satwik's shoulder to recover properly. "We didn't want to aggravate it," he said. "Since we've already got good results, we can take a step back, do rehab, and then focus on the next set of tournaments."

Their return is targeted at the Japan Open and China Open, both of which precede the BWF World Championships — the one major title that has eluded them. Beyond that lies the 2026 Asian Games in Aichi-Nagoya, Japan, where India will look to defend the gold medal that Satwik and Chirag won in Hangzhou in 2022.

The BCCI is not the only Indian sports body sending a full-strength squad to the Asian Games. With badminton being a medal priority for India, the Satwik-Chirag pairing will carry enormous expectations — particularly after their Singapore Open performance proved that the difficult years are behind them.

## The Diaspora Dimension

For Indian-origin fans in the US and UK who follow badminton, the Satwik-Chirag story resonates on a different frequency. Unlike cricket, where India's depth of talent is taken for granted, badminton has always felt more precarious. A single injury, a single bad draw, can derail an Olympic cycle. The fact that this pair survived a two-year wilderness and came back stronger is not just a sporting story — it is a story about persistence, about refusing to let a difficult phase define a career.

As Chirag put it simply: "We kept fighting."
